# 2 Samuel Chapter 16 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 186v–187r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_016_page_001.jpg, 2SA_016_page_002.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** When David had passed a little beyond the summit, behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with a pair of saddled donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred cakes of raisins, a hundred cakes of summer fruit, and a skin of wine.

**2** The king said to Ziba, "What do you mean by these?" Ziba said, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who grow faint in the wilderness to drink."

**3** The king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he is staying in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my father.'"

**4** Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I bow down before you. May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king."

**5** When King David came to Bahurim, behold, a man of the family of the house of Saul came out from there. His name was Shimei the son of Gera, and he came out, cursing continually as he came.

**6** He threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, though all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.

**7** Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!

**8** The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your ruin is upon you, for you are a man of blood!"

**9** Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head."

**10** But the king said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? If he curses, and if the LORD has told him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'"

**11** And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son, who came from my own body, seeks my life. How much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.

**12** It may be that the LORD will look on my affliction and will repay me with good for his cursing this day."

**13** So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him, cursing as he went and throwing stones at him and flinging dust.

**14** The king and all the people who were with him arrived weary, and he refreshed himself there.

**15** Now Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.

**16** When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"

**17** Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"

**18** Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for the one whom the LORD has chosen, and this people, and all the men of Israel — his I will be, and with him I will remain.

**19** And furthermore, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I served before your father, so I will serve before you."

**20** Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give us your counsel. What shall we do?"

**21** Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself odious to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."

**22** So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.

**23** Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one inquired of the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators agree on the chapter's three-part structure: the Ziba encounter (vv.1-4), the Shimei cursing (vv.5-14), and the Jerusalem scenes with Hushai and Ahithophel (vv.15-23). The key theological moment — David's acceptance of Shimei's cursing as potentially from the LORD (vv.10-12) — is handled with consistent care across all three translations. The Ketiv/Qere variant in v.12 is resolved unanimously in favor of the Qere ("my affliction"). The connection between the rooftop scene in v.22 and the Bathsheba narrative in chapter 11 is noted by all three translators.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.2 — "faint" vs. "grow faint" vs. "collapses from exhaustion"
- **EMET:** "the-faint [yya'ef] in-the-wilderness"
- **LOGOS:** "those who grow faint in the wilderness"
- **PNEUMA:** "anyone who collapses from exhaustion in the wilderness"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "those who grow faint in the wilderness." LOGOS captures *ya'ef* (faint/weary) accurately. PNEUMA's "collapses from exhaustion" intensifies beyond what the Hebrew says.

### V.3 — "son of your master" vs. "your master's grandson" vs. "your master's son"
- **EMET:** "the-son of-your-master"
- **LOGOS:** "your master's son"
- **PNEUMA:** "your master's grandson"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "your master's son." The Hebrew *ben adonekha* is literally "son of your master." Mephibosheth is technically Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, but David uses the relational term as it stands. PNEUMA's "grandson" over-specifies.

### V.5 — "coming out and cursing" vs. "cursing continually" vs. "hurling curses nonstop"
- **EMET:** "coming-out, coming-out and-cursing [meqallel]"
- **LOGOS:** "came out, cursing continually as he came"
- **PNEUMA:** "came out hurling curses nonstop"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "came out, cursing continually as he came." LOGOS captures the continuous participle *meqallel* and the emphatic doubling (*yatso yatso*) with "continually." PNEUMA's "nonstop" is too colloquial.

### V.7 — "man of worthlessness" vs. "worthless man" vs. "scoundrel"
- **EMET:** "man of-the-worthless [ish ha-beliyya'al]"
- **LOGOS:** "worthless man"
- **PNEUMA:** "scoundrel"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "worthless man." LOGOS preserves the force of *beliyya'al* in formal English. PNEUMA's "scoundrel" is too mild for a term that carries connotations of utter moral bankruptcy and, in later tradition, demonic evil.

### V.8 — "behold you in your evil" vs. "your ruin is upon you" vs. "Look at you now — ruined!"
- **EMET:** "And-behold-you in-your-evil [ra'ah]"
- **LOGOS:** "See, your ruin is upon you"
- **PNEUMA:** "Look at you now — ruined!"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "See, your ruin is upon you." LOGOS captures the Hebrew *hinnekha bera'atekha* with appropriate formality. The word *ra'ah* means both "evil" and "ruin/disaster" — in context, Shimei declares that David's own wickedness has returned upon him.

### V.10 — "What is to me and to you" vs. "What have I to do with you" vs. "This is not your concern"
- **EMET:** "What [is]-to-me and-to-you"
- **LOGOS:** "What have I to do with you"
- **PNEUMA:** "This is not your concern"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "What have I to do with you." LOGOS preserves the traditional rendering of *mah-li ve-lakhem*, a formula of disassociation that occurs at key moments in David's story and appears in the NT (John 2:4).

### V.12 — Ketiv/Qere: "his eye" vs. "my affliction"
- **EMET:** Notes both readings, translates Ketiv "with-his-eye" with Qere noted
- **LOGOS:** Follows Qere: "my affliction"
- **PNEUMA:** Follows Qere: "how much I'm suffering"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "my affliction." Following the Qere (*be'on'yi*) against the Ketiv (*be'eyniy*). The Qere yields the more coherent reading and accords with the theology of the lament psalms.

### V.13 — "threw dust" vs. "flinging dust" vs. "kicking up clouds of dust"
- **EMET:** "threw-dust [ve'iffer be'afar]"
- **LOGOS:** "flinging dust"
- **PNEUMA:** "kicking up clouds of dust"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "flinging dust." LOGOS is accurate — the Hebrew *'iffer be'afar* means to throw/fling dust. PNEUMA adds "clouds of" and changes the action to "kicking up," neither of which is in the text.

### V.17 — "covenant-faithfulness" vs. "loyalty"
- **EMET:** "your-covenant-faithfulness [chesed]"
- **LOGOS:** "your loyalty"
- **PNEUMA:** "loyalty"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "your loyalty." In this context, Absalom uses *chesed* to mean personal loyalty/faithfulness to a friend. While "covenant-faithfulness" is the project convention for *chesed* in theological contexts, here the word functions as interpersonal fidelity. LOGOS's "loyalty" is contextually appropriate. A footnote noting the Hebrew *chesed* is warranted.

### V.21 — "made yourself odious" vs. "made yourself repulsive"
- **EMET:** "made-yourself-odious [niv'ashta]"
- **LOGOS:** "made yourself odious"
- **PNEUMA:** "made yourself repulsive"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "made yourself odious." EMET/LOGOS correctly render the hithpael of *ba'ash* (to stink/become odious). "Odious" preserves the formal register; PNEUMA's "repulsive" shifts toward physical revulsion rather than social/political offensiveness.

### V.23 — "inquires of the word of God" vs. "carried the weight of a word from God"
- **EMET:** "as-that-which one-inquires [yish'al] of-[the]-word of-God"
- **LOGOS:** "as if one inquired of the word of God"
- **PNEUMA:** "carried the weight of a word from God himself"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "as if one inquired of the word of God." LOGOS preserves the Hebrew simile structure (*ka'asher yish'al*) — the comparison is specifically to the practice of seeking a divine oracle. PNEUMA's rendering changes the simile into a metaphor of "weight."

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
